claim: Nearly 50 different mouse retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types sample the visual scene for distinct features.
source: Nearly 50 different mouse retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types sample the visual scene for distinct features.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on RGC diversity and function.

claim: RGC feature selectivity arises from their synapses with a specific subset of amacrine (AC) and bipolar cell (BC) types.
source: RGC feature selectivity arises from their synapses with a specific subset of amacrine (AC) and bipolar cell (BC) types, but how RGC dendrites arborize and collect input from these specific subsets remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding in the field, supported by the context of the introduction.

claim: Sdk1 is expressed by a family of five RGCs whose dendrites target IPL layers bearing the processes of five Sdk1-expressing interneurons.
source: We show that Sdk1 is expressed by a family of five RGCs whose dendrites target IPL layers bearing the processes of five Sdk1-expressing interneurons (ACs and BCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from histological and molecular characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Sdk1 family includes two ON-direction-selective RGCs.
source: We uncover molecular markers for each Sdk1 RGC and applied these markers following calcium imaging to investigate their visual responses, discovering that the Sdk1 family includes two ON-direction-selective RGCs and an RGC (S1-RGC) sensitive to local edges.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data and molecular marker analysis presented in the results.

claim: The Sdk1 family includes an RGC (S1-RGC) sensitive to local edges.
source: We uncover molecular markers for each Sdk1 RGC and applied these markers following calcium imaging to investigate their visual responses, discovering that the Sdk1 family includes two ON-direction-selective RGCs and an RGC (S1-RGC) sensitive to local edges.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiological data showing S1-RGC responses to edge stimuli.

claim: Loss of Sdk1 disrupted responses to visual stimuli on S1-RGCs without affecting other members of the Sdk1-RGC family.
source: Loss of Sdk1 disrupted responses to visual stimuli on S1-RGCs without affecting other members of the Sdk1-RGC family.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings comparing Sdk1 knockout and control retinae.

claim: Sdk1 loss reduced excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to S1-RGCs.
source: Using electrophysiological recordings, we show that Sdk1 loss reduced excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to S1-RGCs, decreasing its firing to visual stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings measuring excitatory and inhibitory currents in S1-RGCs.

claim: Sdk1 loss decreased S1-RGC firing to visual stimuli.
source: Using electrophysiological recordings, we show that Sdk1 loss reduced excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to S1-RGCs, decreasing its firing to visual stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by loose-patch recordings showing reduced spike responses in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: Stimulus-evoked responses on Sdk1+ ON-alpha RGCs were unaffected by Sdk1 loss.
source: These synaptic deficits were specific to S1-RGCs as stimulus-evoked responses on Sdk1+ ON-alpha RGCs were unaffected by Sdk1 loss.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings from ONα-RGCs in Sdk1 knockout retinae showing normal responses.

claim: The loss of Sdk1 does not alter the IPL layer targeting of S1-RGC dendrites.
source: Finally, we show that the loss of Sdk1 does not alter the IPL layer targeting of S1-RGC dendrites but selectively reduces their intralaminar complexity and size.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of S1-RGC dendritic lamination in control and knockout retinae.

claim: The loss of Sdk1 selectively reduces S1-RGC intralaminar dendritic complexity and size.
source: Finally, we show that the loss of Sdk1 does not alter the IPL layer targeting of S1-RGC dendrites but selectively reduces their intralaminar complexity and size.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing reduced dendritic branch length and arbor area in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop dendritic arbors and receive AC and BC synapses.
source: From our results, we conclude that Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop dendritic arbors and receive AC and BC synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined evidence of reduced dendritic complexity and synaptic inputs in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: Each of the ~46 types of retinal ganglion cell synapses with a unique subset of amacrine and bipolar cell types to create circuits that detect a unique aspect of the visual scene.
source: In the retina, each of the ~46 types of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) synapses with a unique subset of amacrine (AC) and bipolar cell (BC) types to create circuits that detect a unique aspect of the visual scene (Clark and Demb, 2016; Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Jadzinsky and Baccus, 2013; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Shekhar et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on RGC diversity and circuit organization.

claim: Recognition molecules guide the neurites of newborn retinal neurons to grow into sublayers of the inner plexiform layer where they contact hundreds of potential synaptic targets.
source: A growing body of work suggests that recognition molecules guide the neurites of newborn retinal neurons to grow into sublayers of a specialized neuropil, the inner plexiform layer (IPL), where they contact hundreds of potential synaptic targets (Rangel Olguin et al., 2020; Sanes and Yamagata, 2009; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on molecular guidance mechanisms in retinal development.

claim: Peter's principle posited that developing neurons synapse with nearby cells according to how often they make contact.
source: An initial idea, called Peter's principle, posited that developing neurons synapse with nearby cells according to how often they make contact (Binzegger et al., 2004; Peters and Feldman, 1976; Shepherd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a historical scientific hypothesis cited from published literature.

claim: Recent connectomic studies of the IPL demonstrate no obvious relationship between contact frequency and synapse number.
source: However, recent connectomic studies of the IPL demonstrate no obvious relationship between contact frequency and synapse number (Briggman et al., 2011; Helmstaedter et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to connectomic studies that challenge Peter's principle.

claim: Connectomic data support a model in which neurons recognize targets in their immediate vicinity and synapse specifically with them.
source: Instead, these connectomic data support a model in which neurons recognize targets in their immediate vicinity and synapse specifically with them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the connectomic studies cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Key molecules in the recognition process are thought to be members of the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSFs).
source: Key molecules in this recognition process are thought to be members of the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSFs).
evidence: This is a statement of current scientific understanding in the field.

claim: IgSFs are adhesion molecules that bind to themselves (homophilic) or compatible IgSFs (heterophilic) across cell-cell junctions.
source: Briefly, IgSFs are adhesion molecules that bind to themselves (homophilic) or compatible IgSFs (heterophilic) across cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This is a statement of established molecular biology knowledge about IgSF proteins.

claim: Selective IgSF expression within synaptic partners allows their neurites to adhere and synapse when they encounter each other.
source: It has been proposed that selective IgSF expression within synaptic partners allows their neurites to adhere and synapse when they encounter each other (Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature about IgSF function in synapse formation.

claim: Sidekick-2 (Sdk2) in VG3-ACs and W3B RGCs drives these neurons to connect with each other far more than they connect with Sdk2-negative neurons they contact.
source: In this study, the IgSF Sidekick-2 (Sdk2) in VG3-ACs and W3B RGCs drives these neurons to connect with each other far more than they connect with the Sdk2-negative neurons they contact.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Krishnaswamy et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of Sdk2 ablates the enhanced VG3-W3B connectivity but does not alter the gross structure or overlap of their arbors.
source: Loss of Sdk2 ablates the enhanced VG3-W3B connectivity but does not alter the gross structure or overlap of their arbors, suggesting that IgSFs increase the probability of synapses between this pair (Krishnaswamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Direction-selective RGCs require the IgSF contactin 5 (Cntn5) to grow dendritic branches in IPL layers bearing axons of their AC/BC partners.
source: On the other hand, direction-selective RGCs require the IgSF contactin 5 (Cntn5) to grow dendritic branches in IPL layers bearing axons of their AC/BC partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Peng et al., 2017).

claim: Loss of Cntn5 from direction-selective RGCs decreases their dendritic branches and reduces synaptic input.
source: Loss of Cntn5 from these RGCs decreases their dendritic branches and reduces synaptic input (Peng et al., 2017), suggesting that IgSFs influence connectivity by regulating intralaminar dendritic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Sdk1 is expressed by subsets of neurons expressing the BC marker Chx10, the AC marker Ap2-α, and the RGC marker RBPMS.
source: Cross-sections and whole mounts from these animals showed GFP+ nuclei within subsets of neurons expressing the BC marker Chx10, the AC marker Ap2-α, and the RGC marker RBPMS (Figure 1A–F); no labeling was found in horizontal cells and photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1A-F.

claim: No Sdk1 labeling was found in horizontal cells and photoreceptors.
source: Cross-sections and whole mounts from these animals showed GFP+ nuclei within subsets of neurons expressing the BC marker Chx10, the AC marker Ap2-α, and the RGC marker RBPMS (Figure 1A–F); no labeling was found in horizontal cells and photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a negative result from the immunohistochemical experiments.

claim: There are approximately 7795 Sdk1-BCs per mm2.
source: Counting double-labeled cells showed ~7795 Sdk1-BCs//mm2, ~350 Sdk1-ACs /mm2, and ~390/mm2 Sdk1-RGCs (Figure 1G), suggesting that Sdk1 labels several retinal circuits.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cell counting experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There are approximately 350 Sdk1-ACs per mm2.
source: Counting double-labeled cells showed ~7795 Sdk1-BCs//mm2, ~350 Sdk1-ACs /mm2, and ~390/mm2 Sdk1-RGCs (Figure 1G), suggesting that Sdk1 labels several retinal circuits.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cell counting experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There are approximately 390 Sdk1-RGCs per mm2.
source: Counting double-labeled cells showed ~7795 Sdk1-BCs//mm2, ~350 Sdk1-ACs /mm2, and ~390/mm2 Sdk1-RGCs (Figure 1G), suggesting that Sdk1 labels several retinal circuits.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cell counting experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Sdk1 is highly expressed in approximately six RGC clusters according to single RGC sequencing atlases.
source: Publicly available single RGC sequencing atlases indicate that Sdk1 is highly expressed in approximately six RGC clusters (Rheaume et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published RGC sequencing atlases.

claim: Two Sdk1 RGC clusters correspond to alpha RGCs with sustained responses to light onset (ONα-RGCs) and type 2 melanopsin-positive RGCs (M2-RGCs).
source: Two clusters correspond to alpha RGCs with sustained responses to light onset (ONα-RGCs) and type 2 melanopsin-positive RGCs (M2-RGCs).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequencing data from published atlases.

claim: Four Sdk1 RGC clusters predicted novel RGC types.
source: Four others predicted novel RGCs types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ost+/Nefh+ RGCs bore large somas and wide dendritic arbors confined to IPL sublamina 5 and matched previous descriptions of ONα-RGCs.
source: Staining retinae from these mice with our panel of molecular markers revealed the morphology of two Sdk1-RGCs: (1) Ost+/Nefh+ RGCs bore large somas and wide dendritic arbors confined to IPL sublamina 5 and matched previous descriptions of ONα-RGCs (Figure 1L and P; Krieger et al., 2017; Krishnaswamy et al., 2015);
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1L and P and comparison to published descriptions.

claim: Brn3c+ RGCs had small somas and grew dendritic arbors confined to the center of sublamina 3.
source: and (2) Brn3c+ RGCs had small somas and grew dendritic arbors confined to the center of sublamina 3 (Figure 1M and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1M and Q.

claim: Only a subset of Sdk1-RGCs project strongly to the LGN and SC.
source: These results suggest that only a subset of Sdk1-RGCs project strongly to the LGN and SC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and D).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that some Sdk1-RGCs were rarely labeled by retrograde viral injections in LGN/SC.

claim: Reporter-labeled RGC axons were found in the non-image-forming medial terminal nucleus (MTN) and olivary pretectal nuclei (OPN).
source: Consistent with this idea, brain sections taken from intraocularly infected Sdk1CG mice showed reporter-labeled RGC axons in the non-image-forming medial terminal nucleus (MTN) and olivary pretectal nuclei (OPN; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Both Nr2f2+/Calb+ and Nr2f2+/Calb- RGCs grew oblong dendritic arbors confined to IPL sublamina 4.
source: These experiments revealed that both Nr2f2+/Calb+ and Nr2f2+/Calb- RGCs grew oblong dendritic arbors confined to IPL sublamina 4 (Figure 1N, R, O and S).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1N, R, O and S.

claim: Sdk1 labels a family of five RGCs, which include image- and non-image-forming types.
source: Thus, Sdk1 labels a family of five RGCs, which include image- and non-image-forming types.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the anatomical and molecular characterization data presented.

claim: One Sdk1-AC had very large (>1 mm) diameter dendritic arbors located in sublamina 5.
source: One of these had very large (>1 mm) diameter dendritic arbors located in sublamina 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A),
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: One Sdk1-AC had a similarly large arbor located in sublamina 3 and resembled descriptions of type 2 catacholaminergic ACs.
source: another had a similarly large arbor located in sublamina 3 and resembled descriptions of type 2 catacholaminergic ACs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B; Knop et al., 2014; Krishnaswamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and comparison to published descriptions.

claim: A third Sdk1-AC grew comparatively narrower dendritic arbors that exhibited the characteristic waterfall appearance of the A17 AC.
source: A third Sdk1-AC grew comparatively narrower dendritic arbors that exhibited the characteristic waterfall appearance of the A17 AC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C; Masland, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and comparison to published descriptions.

claim: Sdk1 labels many rod BCs as judged by their anatomy.
source: Cross-sections from the same experiments also showed the presence of many rod BCs as judged by their anatomy (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D),
evidence: This claim is based on morphological identification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Sdk1 labels many BCs that targeted the interface between sublamina 3 and 4, matching reports of type 7 BCs.
source: as well as many BCs that targeted the interface between sublamina 3 and 4, matching reports of type 7 BCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E; Wassle et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E and comparison to published descriptions.

claim: Sdk1-ACs, BCs, and RGCs target a common set of IPL laminae.
source: The IPL lamination profiles of Sdk1-ACs, BCs, and RGCs show that these cells target a common set of IPL laminae.
evidence: This is an inference from the lamination data presented for Sdk1-expressing neurons.

claim: Sdk1 defines a family of neurons whose circuits are contained within the inner three layers of the IPL.
source: Thus, we conclude that Sdk1 defines a family of neurons whose circuits are contained within the inner three layers of the IPL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lamination patterns observed for Sdk1-expressing neurons.

claim: Ost+ RGCs (M2- and Onα- RGCs) showed sustained responses to the onset of a full-field flash and leading edge of the moving bar.
source: Ost+ RGCs (M2- and Onα- RGCs) showed sustained responses to the onset of a full-field flash and leading edge of the moving bar.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the results.

claim: Ost+ RGCs showed weak directional tuning with no systematic preference for stimuli moving along any cardinal axis.
source: Converting each polar plot to a direction-selective index (DSI) and preferred angle and viewing the entire Ost+ population on polar axes confirmed this picture, showing weak directional tuning with no systematic preference for stimuli moving along any cardinal axis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ost+ RGCs lack motion selectivity.
source: Comparing the average DSI within this group for fast- or slow-moving bars was similar, indicating a lack of motion selectivity within the Ost+ RGC group (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both Nr2f2+ RGC types gave transient responses to the leading edge of the moving bar that varied systematically with bar direction.
source: On the other hand, both Nr2f2+ RGC types gave transient responses to the leading edge of the moving bar that varied systematically with bar direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the results.

claim: Nr2f2+/Calb+ RGCs showed polar plots that pointed ventrally.
source: Aligning these responses to retinal orientation revealed polar plots that pointed ventrally for Nr2f2+/Calb+ RGCs (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nr2+/Calb- RGCs showed polar plots pointing dorsally.
source: or moving dorsally for Nr2+/Calb- RGCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Reducing bar velocity caused the average DSI of both Nr2f2+ RGC types to increase.
source: DSI polar plots for these two populations showed the same respective biases for ventral or dorsal motion and reducing bar velocity caused the average DSI of both RGC types to increase (Figure 2F), indicating that Nr2f2+ RGCs encode the direction of slow-moving bright stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI analysis at different bar velocities shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Nr2f2+ RGCs encode the direction of slow-moving bright stimuli.
source: DSI polar plots for these two populations showed the same respective biases for ventral or dorsal motion and reducing bar velocity caused the average DSI of both RGC types to increase (Figure 2F), indicating that Nr2f2+ RGCs encode the direction of slow-moving bright stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the DSI analysis showing increased selectivity for slow-moving bars.

claim: Nr2f2+ RGCs strongly resemble ON-direction-selective RGCs (ON-DSGCs).
source: Taken together with our anatomical results, Nr2f2+ RGCs strongly resemble ON-direction-selective RGCs (ON-DSGCs), which grow dendrites in sublamina 4 and comprise three subtypes attuned to motion toward either dorsal, ventral, and nasal poles of the retina (Dhande et al., 2013; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Yonehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional and anatomical properties of Nr2f2+ RGCs compared to published descriptions of ON-DSGCs.

claim: Approximately 3% of Pcdh9-Cre reporter-labeled cells overlap with ventral motion-selective Nr2f2+/Calb+ RGCs.
source: Staining reporter-labeled retinae from the Pcdh9-Cre line, which marks ventrally tuned ON-DSGCs (Lilley et al., 2019; Matsumoto and Yonehara, 2018), showed overlap with ventral motion-selective Nr2f2+/Calb+ RGCs (~3% of reporter-labeled cells; 1035 Pcdh9-Cre cells/mm2; Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Nr2f2+ RGCs likely correspond to a pair of ON-DSGCs.
source: Thus, we conclude that Nr2f2+ RGCs likely correspond to a pair of ON-DSGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional, anatomical, and molecular evidence presented.

claim: S1-RGCs (Brn3c+) showed ON responses to a full-field flash but responded to both the leading and trailing edge of the bright moving bar.
source: S1-RGCs (Brn3c+) showed ON responses to a full-field flash but responded to both the leading and trailing edge of the bright moving bar (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: S1-RGCs can respond to both bright and dark stimuli.
source: These results indicate that S1-RGCs can respond to both bright and dark stimuli and suggest that large full-field stimuli may recruit surround mechanisms that attenuate S1-RGC responses.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that S1-RGCs respond to both leading and trailing edges of moving bars.

claim: Large full-field stimuli may recruit surround mechanisms that attenuate S1-RGC responses.
source: These results indicate that S1-RGCs can respond to both bright and dark stimuli and suggest that large full-field stimuli may recruit surround mechanisms that attenuate S1-RGC responses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the difference between full-field and moving bar responses.

claim: Many S1-RGCs respond best to bars traveling slowly (200 μm/s) along the same axis.
source: Plotting S1-RGC bar responses against bar direction showed that many cells respond best to bars traveling slowly (200 μm/s) along the same axis, suggesting that these neurons detect stimulus orientation (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E and H.

claim: S1-RGCs detect stimulus orientation.
source: Plotting S1-RGC bar responses against bar direction showed that many cells respond best to bars traveling slowly (200 μm/s) along the same axis, suggesting that these neurons detect stimulus orientation (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that S1-RGCs respond preferentially to bars moving along a single axis.

claim: S1-RGCs show higher orientational preference compared to other Sdk1-RGCs.
source: Computing an orientation selectivity index (OSI) for these cells showed a higher orientational preference in this neuron as compared with the other Sdk1-RGCs (Figure 2G);
evidence: This claim is supported by OSI analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: S1-RGC OSI values are significantly weaker than the OSI found in recently described orientation-selective RGCs.
source: however, these values are significantly weaker than the OSI found in recently described orientation-selective RGCs (Nath and Schwartz, 2016; Nath and Schwartz, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data on orientation-selective RGCs.

claim: S1-RGCs are ON-OFF cells that respond best to edges that fall within their receptive fields.
source: Thus, we conclude that S1-RGCs are ON-OFF cells that respond best to edges that fall within their receptive fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional characterization of S1-RGCs.

claim: The responses of Sdk1-null Ost+ RGCs resembled their heterozygote counterparts.
source: The responses of Sdk1-null Ost+ RGCs, which include Onα- and M2-RGCs, resembled their heterozygote counterparts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing Sdk1 knockout and control Ost+ RGCs shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nr2f2+ RGCs showed subtle changes in their average responses to full-field and moving bar stimuli in Sdk1 nulls.
source: Nr2f2+ RGCs, which include two kinds of ON-DSGCs, showed subtle changes in their average responses to full-field and moving bar stimuli (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Nr2f2+ RGCs showed altered directional preference and selectivity in Sdk1 nulls, particularly in the NR2f2+/Calb+ group.
source: with altered directional preference and selectivity, particularly in the NR2f2+/Calb+ group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: S1-RGCs were most affected by Sdk1 loss and showed a significant decrease in response magnitude to bar stimuli.
source: S1-RGCs were most affected by Sdk1 loss and showed a significant decrease in response magnitude to bar stimuli (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sdk1 loss strongly impairs S1-RGCs.
source: These results indicate that Sdk1 loss strongly impairs S1-RGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional deficits observed in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: Single-cell sequencing data showed high levels of Sdk2 in other Sdk1-RGCs relative to S1-RGCs.
source: Interestingly, single-cell sequencing data showed high levels of Sdk2 in other Sdk1-RGCs relative to S1-RGCs, suggesting that there could be functional redundancy in Onα-, M2-, and ON-DSGCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There could be functional redundancy between Sdk1 and Sdk2 in Onα-, M2-, and ON-DSGCs.
source: Interestingly, single-cell sequencing data showed high levels of Sdk2 in other Sdk1-RGCs relative to S1-RGCs, suggesting that there could be functional redundancy in Onα-, M2-, and ON-DSGCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the Sdk2 expression pattern in different Sdk1-RGC types.

claim: S1-RGCs showed ON and OFF responses to a moving bar that were strongest for motion along a single axis.
source: S1-RGCs were easily targeted for loose-patch recordings by their small soma and showed ON and OFF responses to a moving bar that were strongest for motion along a single axis as judged by their elongated profiles on a polar plot (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: ONα-RGCs showed sustained responses to light onset with little tuning for motion direction.
source: Similar recordings from nearby large-soma ONα-RGCs showed sustained responses to light onset with little tuning for motion direction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Control S1-RGCs showed ON and OFF responses to an expanding spot that were strongly suppressed by spot size.
source: S1-RGCs showed ON and OFF responses to this stimulus that were strongly suppressed by spot size, with OFF responses nearly silenced by spots exceeding ~300 μm (Figure 4D, F, G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D, F, G.

claim: Both ON and OFF components of S1-RGCs were most strongly activated by spot sizes close to the diameter of S1-RGC dendritic arbors.
source: Both ON and OFF components were most strongly activated by spot sizes close to the diameter of S1-RGC dendritic arbors, indicating that the receptive field center on these neurons is ~120–150 μm (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The receptive field center on S1-RGCs is approximately 120-150 μm.
source: Both ON and OFF components were most strongly activated by spot sizes close to the diameter of S1-RGC dendritic arbors, indicating that the receptive field center on these neurons is ~120–150 μm (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is an inference from the spot size tuning data.

claim: Sdk1 heterozygote ONα-RGCs displayed higher baseline spiking than S1-RGCs and sustained ON responses that were poorly suppressed by large stimuli.
source: Recordings from Sdk1 heterozygote ONα-RGCs displayed higher baseline spiking than S1-RGCs and sustained ON responses that were poorly suppressed by large stimuli (Figure 4E), consistent with their full-field and moving bar responses in our calcium imaging experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Wild-type Onα-RGCs showed similar responses to Sdk1 heterozygote Onα-RGCs.
source: Similar responses were found in wild-type Onα-RGCs, bearing two copies of Sdk1, labeled with the Kcng4-Cre line crossed to Cre-dependent reporters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: S1-RGCs in Sdk1 null retinae showed a dramatic loss of responsivity to dark stimuli and significantly weaker responses to ON stimuli.
source: In contrast, the same recordings from S1-RGCs in Sdk1CG/CG retinae showed a dramatic loss of responsivity to dark stimuli and significantly weaker responses to ON stimuli (Figure 4D, F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D, F, G.

claim: Sdk1-null ONα-RGCs showed comparable responses to their control counterparts.
source: Recordings from nearby Sdk1-null ONα-RGCs showed comparable responses to their control counterparts (Figure 4E and H), indicating that Sdk1 loss selectively affects S1-RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E and H.

claim: Sdk1 loss selectively affects S1-RGCs.
source: Recordings from nearby Sdk1-null ONα-RGCs showed comparable responses to their control counterparts (Figure 4E and H), indicating that Sdk1 loss selectively affects S1-RGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Sdk1 knockout effects on S1-RGCs versus ONα-RGCs.

claim: S1-RGCs responded preferentially to both bright and dark bars oriented along a single axis.
source: As expected from their responses to moving bars, S1-RGCs responded preferentially to both bright and dark bars oriented along a single axis (Figure 4I), whereas Onα-RGCs respond to bright bars alone with little response variation to bar orientation (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Onα-RGCs respond to bright bars alone with little response variation to bar orientation.
source: As expected from their responses to moving bars, S1-RGCs responded preferentially to both bright and dark bars oriented along a single axis (Figure 4I), whereas Onα-RGCs respond to bright bars alone with little response variation to bar orientation (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Oriented bar stimuli evoked poor responses from S1-RGCs in Sdk1 null retinae.
source: The same stimulus evoked poor responses from S1-RGCs in Sdk1CG/CG retinae (Figure 4I,K,L), with significantly weaker responses to dark and bright bars, confirming our results using bright and dark expanding spot stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4I, K, L.

claim: Sdk1 null S1-RGCs showed significantly weaker responses to dark and bright oriented bars.
source: The same stimulus evoked poor responses from S1-RGCs in Sdk1CG/CG retinae (Figure 4I,K,L), with significantly weaker responses to dark and bright bars, confirming our results using bright and dark expanding spot stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4I, K, L.

claim: Sdk1-null Onα-RGCs showed similar responses to oriented bars as controls.
source: The same recordings from nearby Sdk1-null Onα-RGCs showed similar responses to those in controls (Figure 4J and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4J and M.

claim: Sdk1 loss caused a selective reduction of orientation selectivity for S1-RGCs.
source: Computing OSI values for these cells and comparing the mean OSI for S1-RGCs and ONα-RGCs in controls and knockout retina showed a selective reduction of orientation selectivity for S1-RGCs in the absence of Sdk1 (Figure 4N).
evidence: This claim is supported by OSI analysis shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop normal responses to visual stimuli.
source: Thus, we conclude that Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop normal responses to visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional deficits observed in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: S1-RGCs in controls showed inward (excitatory) currents at –60 mV to both bright and dark spots that grew in strength until the spot reached ~150 μm in diameter and then steadily weakened.
source: S1-RGCs in controls showed inward (excitatory) currents at –60 mV to both bright and dark spots that grew in strength until the spot reached ~150 μm in diameter and then steadily weakened (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: S1-RGCs in controls showed outward (inhibitory) currents at 0 mV to both bright and dark spots that grew steadily with spot diameter.
source: Outward (inhibitory) currents at 0 mV were also found to both bright and dark spots but grew steadily with spot diameter (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: S1-RGCs in Sdk1 null retinae showed significantly weaker inward and outward currents to bright and dark spots at all spot diameters.
source: Recordings from S1-RGCs in SdkCG/CG retinae showed significantly weaker inward and outward currents to bright and dark spots at all spot diameters (Figure 5A–F), indicating a loss of functional excitatory and inhibitory synapses on S1-RGCs in the absence of Sdk1.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Sdk1 loss causes a loss of functional excitatory and inhibitory synapses on S1-RGCs.
source: Recordings from S1-RGCs in SdkCG/CG retinae showed significantly weaker inward and outward currents to bright and dark spots at all spot diameters (Figure 5A–F), indicating a loss of functional excitatory and inhibitory synapses on S1-RGCs in the absence of Sdk1.
evidence: This is an inference from the reduced synaptic currents observed in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: ONα-RGCs showed similar inward and outward currents between controls and knockouts.
source: Whole-cell recordings from nearby ONα-RGCs showed inward and outward currents that were similar between controls and knockouts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that Sdk1 loss impairs synaptic inputs on S1-RGCs rather than generally affecting excitatory and inhibitory synaptic strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Sdk1 loss impairs synaptic inputs on S1-RGCs rather than generally affecting excitatory and inhibitory synaptic strength.
source: Whole-cell recordings from nearby ONα-RGCs showed inward and outward currents that were similar between controls and knockouts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that Sdk1 loss impairs synaptic inputs on S1-RGCs rather than generally affecting excitatory and inhibitory synaptic strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of synaptic currents in S1-RGCs versus ONα-RGCs in Sdk1 knockouts.

claim: Control S1-RGCs showed inward and outward currents to both bright and dark oriented bars, with magnitudes varying with bar orientation.
source: Controls showed inward and outward currents to both bright and dark oriented bars, but the magnitudes of these currents varied with bar orientation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Orientations that produced the strongest excitation in S1-RGCs were orthogonal to those producing the strongest inhibition.
source: Integrating these currents across the presentation time of each bar and normalizing the responses showed a systematic change in stimulus-evoked charge with bar angle. Orientations that produced the strongest excitation were orthogonal to those producing the strongest inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of integrated synaptic currents shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: Oriented bar stimuli evoked significantly weaker inward and outward currents from S1-RGCs in Sdk1 null retinae.
source: The same stimulus evoked significantly weaker inward and outward currents from S1-RGCs in Sdk1CG/CG retinae, consistent with their reduced responses to the expanding spot stimulus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, D,G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, D, G-I.

claim: Excitatory currents in Sdk1 null S1-RGCs retained their preference for bar orientation, but the tuning of inhibitory inputs became less selective.
source: Integrating these responses across stimulus presentation time and normalizing these responses to the average maximal response in controls showed that excitatory currents retained their preference for bar orientation, but the tuning of inhibitory inputs became less selective (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of integrated synaptic currents shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G-I.

claim: Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs.
source: Thus, we conclude that Sdk1 is required for S1-RGCs to develop excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the synaptic current deficits observed in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: The laminar position of S1-RGC dendrites showed no obvious difference between controls and Sdk1 nulls.
source: However, comparing the laminar position of S1-RGC dendrites in Sdk1CG/+ or Sdk1CG/CG retinal cross-sections showed no obvious difference between controls and nulls (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The loss of Sdk1 led S1-RGCs to grow dendritic arbors that were less complex than their control counterparts.
source: We found that the loss of Sdk1 led S1-RGCs to grow dendritic arbors that were less complex than their control counterparts (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Sdk1-null S1-RGC arbors contained similar numbers of dendritic branches as controls.
source: Sdk1-null S1-RGC arbors contained similar numbers of dendritic branches (Figure 5J),
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Sdk1-null S1-RGC dendritic branches were approximately half as long on average as controls.
source: but they were approximately half as long on average, which led to fewer intersections across the entire dendritic arbor as assessed by Sholl analysis (Figure 5K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 5K-M.

claim: Reduced S1-RGC dendritic arbor size did not alter the spatial distribution of these neurons.
source: Reduced S1-RGC dendritic arbor size did not alter the spatial distribution of these neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by density recovery profile analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Sdk1 loss caused dendritic deficits in S1-RGCs with little gross change in the overall structure of the IPL.
source: These deficits arose with little gross change in the overall structure of the IPL, as assessed by staining with a variety of markers that label AC and BC subsets targeting specific sublayers (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reconstructed ONα-RGCs in Sdk1 null retinae showed subtler deficits and more closely resembled their counterparts in heterozygote retinae.
source: Reconstructed ONα-RGCs in the same Sdk1CG/CG retina showed subtler deficits and more closely resembled their counterparts in heterozygote retinae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-H.

claim: Heterozygote Onα-RGCs resembled wild-type Onα-RGCs labeled with the KCNG4-Cre line.
source: Heterozygote Onα-RGCs in turn resembled wild-type Onα-RGCs labeled with the KCNG4-Cre line, supporting our functional observations, and suggesting that retinae bearing one or two copies of Sdk1 are similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sdk1 loss impairs S1-RGCs dendritic arborization.
source: Taken together, these results show that Sdk1 loss impairs S1-RGCs dendritic arborization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the morphological deficits observed in Sdk1 knockout S1-RGCs.

claim: Sdk1 shapes dendrite growth and wiring to help S1-RGCs become feature selective.
source: We conclude that Sdk1 shapes dendrite growth and wiring to help S1-RGCs become feature selective.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the functional and structural data presented.

claim: S1-RGCs most closely resemble type 1 or type 2 high-definition RGCs (HD1 or HD2).
source: Of these, S1-RGCs most closely resemble type 1 or type 2 high-definition RGCs (HD1 or HD2).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously described RGC types based on functional properties.

claim: S1-RGCs show sensitivity to edge orientation, which could arise from their orthogonally tuned excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: However, S1-RGCs also show sensitivity to edge orientation, which could arise from their orthogonally tuned excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying S1-RGC orientation sensitivity.

claim: Sdk1 loss causes a significant loss of S1-RGC responsivity with smaller effects on the other Sdk1-RGC types.
source: In the second section, we found that Sdk1 loss caused a significant loss of S1-RGC responsivity with smaller effects on the other Sdk1-RGC types.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional results comparing different Sdk1-RGC types in knockouts.

claim: Sdk1 is required for the dendritic and synaptic development of a local edge-detecting RGC type.
source: We conclude that Sdk1 is required for the dendritic and synaptic development of a local edge-detecting RGC type.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
